Yeah. My question is: With respect to the pre-pandemic, I'd say before 2020, and in the year '23, what have been the trends on missed collections and dirty conditions and sanitation connections?

Okay. So missed collections was an area of obsessive focus for me and for the department over the last year. Our agency, at its core, we are a customer service agency and a really good way to piss your customer off is to leave trash in front of their house. And so we have been incredibly focused on driving down the number of missed collections. Trash dash has been extremely helpful to that end, because all of a sudden there is full transparency in the data. Our superintendents, and our chiefs, and everyone in management can see exactly where the missed collections were on a day by day, week by week basis. We can spot patterns and trends, and this is a big topic of conversation at our trash dash meeting. On our most recent trash dash report, our missed collections, week to date -- so for comparing calendar year 2024 to calendar year 2023, this week or last week -- down 50%. And it just goes to show that when you focus on the right things, you have good data behind them, and a strategy designed based on that data, you can make real progress. And missed collections is definitely an area where we have really great progress.

So this is like definitely not just like a one week sampling of data that I am looking about. Dirty conditions in the city, I would say, are down since the pandemic, when there was absolutely no street cleaning going on or, like, if any virtually little, very little, virtually no street cleaning going on at the Department of Sanitation. And now we have a number of initiatives designed specifically to address dirty conditions. So among them, our targeted neighborhood task force. There are what we call No Man's Lands, historically No Man's Lands, city-owned property. That was the jurisdiction of no one, no agency to clean historically. Mayor Adams made a historic investment in creating this targeted neighborhood task force inside the Department of Sanitation, and we have about 100 sanitation workers every day that spend their time cleaning those historically forgotten parts of the city. They're in almost-- they're certainly in every borough in virtually every neighborhood in the city, underpasses

And if you look at what the MTA has done with the bus lanes, where they have now automated ticketing systems that enforce bus lanes, if we put these automated ticketing systems on our street sweepers, people would move their car, because the manual enforcement of alternate side parking, yes, of course is important.
